subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
subtype: Approach: rethink the semester load with a leave option [Revision]
passage:
Honestly, I thought it would be over by the spring. Mum's illness was supposed to be a few weeks, and I planned to keep my full load of six courses. Then the weeks became months, and I began to fail quizzes I would normally ace.

I'm Yash. In October I made an appointment with my adviser, Leela, and put my transcript on her desk. I said, "I can't do six anymore, and I don't want to fail all of them." She didn't lecture me. We looked at the options together, and I decided to drop to three courses this term and take the next one off, with a written plan to return in January.

It felt like giving something up. But it was better than three failed grades, and Mum was glad I chose it.

qa.q: How many courses did Yash keep for this term?
qa.a: Three courses this term.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling in the weeks when quizzes were failing?
qa.a: Yash felt overwhelmed and worried, seeing marks slip that would normally be strong and realising the plan was no longer working.

qa.q: What could Yash do to make the return in January easier, and why?
qa.a: Yash could keep in touch with Leela during the break and review the written plan, because staying connected makes it easier to restart.

qa.q: How might Leela see Yash's decision to come in?
qa.a: Leela probably sees a student who acted early and honestly, which makes it easier to find a solution before the grades suffer.

grounding: When the illness lasts longer, the student meets an adviser and reduces the course load, with a plan to return.

subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
subtype: Approach: avoid telling the college and hide poor results [Pitfall]
passage:
Wednesday, late.

Got the attendance notice from the department today. "Shortage of attendance: standard penalty applies." Standard penalty. As though I'd been bunking to sit in a cafe. I've missed eleven classes because Mum's treatment days keep landing on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and I haven't told a single teacher. What would I even say? That my family is a mess?

Aparna, who sits next to me, asked quietly at lunch why I look so tired and why I keep disappearing. I said I was fine and changed the subject. My last two test marks fell, and now this. They can't help because they don't know. And the more I hide, the more it costs.

Tarun

qa.q: How many classes has Tarun missed?
qa.a: Eleven classes.

qa.q: What is Tarun feeling about telling the teachers?
qa.a: Tarun feels ashamed and afraid of being judged, which is why the question of what to say leaves Tarun silent.

qa.q: What could Tarun do about the attendance notice, and why?
qa.a: Tarun could go to a teacher or the department with the notice and explain the treatment days, because the department can only adjust things it knows about.

qa.q: How might Aparna see Tarun's disappearing and tired looks?
qa.a: Aparna sees a classmate who is clearly struggling and cares enough to ask, though Aparna may feel shut out by the answer 'fine'.

grounding: Fearing judgement, the student tells the college nothing, misses classes without explanation, and standard penalties follow.

subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
subtype: Approach: learn from hospital staff how to help at home [Action]
passage:
In Addis Ababa, Abebe stood at the foot of his father's hospital bed, watching the ward nurse, Leila, shift a patient with one smooth movement. He had been lifting his father at home by the arms, and his own back hurt.

He asked, "Could you show me how you do it?" Leila smiled and demonstrated: bend the knees, keep the back straight, turn together with the patient. She let him try it twice with her hand near his. Then she talked him through the diet sheet, what to offer and what to avoid, and he wrote it all in a small notebook.

At home that weekend, his father settled more easily, and Abebe's back stopped aching.

qa.q: What did Abebe ask Leila to show him?
qa.a: How she moves a patient.

qa.q: How was Abebe feeling as he watched Leila at the bedside?
qa.a: Abebe felt worried and unsure, seeing his own way of lifting was hurting his back and hoping to do better for his father.

qa.q: What could Abebe do if he forgets a step at home, and why?
qa.a: Abebe could check the notebook and phone the ward to ask Leila to repeat it, because a nurse can correct a detail before it becomes a problem.

qa.q: How might Leila see a family member asking to learn?
qa.a: Leila likely feels glad to see a relative who wants to do it safely, since helping him learn makes the patient's care better after leaving.

grounding: The student asks nurses to show safe lifting and diet instructions and writes them down, making home care safer.

subtype: Approach: implementation intention with a fixed cue [Thinking]
passage:
Dear Lavanya,

You asked how I finally started walking every day when I had failed all last year. Here is my thinking. I used to say, "I'll walk sometime today," and "sometime" never came. Every day I had to decide when, and by evening I was tired and had no energy for the decision.

So I wrote one sentence on a card: When the toothbrush goes back in the cup each morning, I walk for twenty minutes. No deciding, no bargaining. The teeth part happens anyway, and the walk hangs on it like a coat on a hook.

On a rushed day it might shrink, but the sentence stays. Twelve mornings so far.

Shreya

qa.q: What is the sentence that Shreya wrote on the card?
qa.a: When the toothbrush goes back in the cup each morning, I walk for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling each evening when 'sometime today' never came, and why?
qa.a: Shreya was drained and probably discouraged, since deciding every single day used up the energy by evening.

qa.q: What could Shreya do if a morning is truly rushed, and why?
qa.a: Shreya could still step outside for a few minutes, because keeping the link to brushing teeth protects the habit even when the walk is short.

qa.q: How might Lavanya feel on receiving this letter?
qa.a: Lavanya may feel curious and pleased that the question got such a thoughtful answer, and may want to try a card of Lavanya's own.

grounding: The person links a walk to an existing morning routine, so the habit no longer needs a daily decision.

subtype: Approach: start with a tiny version that can be done on bad days [Action]
passage:
I'm Nikita, and I used to believe that if a workout wasn't an hour, it didn't count. So I did nothing for months. Then Vishal, my flatmate, said, "Just do ten minutes. Even when you feel awful."

So the first week I stretched for ten minutes, then jogged slowly to the end of the lane and back. It was almost embarrassing. But on the bad days, when I had a headache or a long day, I could still do that. The next week I added two minutes. The week after, two more.

Now it's forty minutes, three mornings a week, and I've not missed since the start. I didn't get fit by being brave. I got here by being small enough that I couldn't say no.

qa.q: How long was the first workout?
qa.a: Stretching for ten minutes, then a slow jog to the end of the lane and back.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel about the tiny first workout?
qa.a: Nikita found it almost embarrassing, though the small size meant it could be done even on bad days.

qa.q: What could Nikita do on a day when even ten minutes seems too much, and why?
qa.a: Nikita could do just the stretching or step outside for a minute, because keeping the chain unbroken matters more than the size of the session.

qa.q: How might Vishal see Nikita's progress?
qa.a: Vishal probably feels quietly pleased, having given the simple advice, and sees Nikita's steady mornings as proof that small steps last.

grounding: The person begins with ten minutes of stretching and a short jog instead of an hour at the gym, adding time each week.

subtype: Approach: all-or-nothing plan with a five-day-a-week gym [Pitfall]
passage:
1 January. Tanvir came home with a receipt for a year's gym membership and a schedule stuck to the fridge: five days a week, hard sessions, no excuses. His cousin Aparna raised an eyebrow. "Start smaller?" "No. Go big or nothing," he said.

19 January. Tanvir had caught a cold, and work was heavy that week. He missed three sessions. On the fridge, the days he'd crossed off had gaps, and the streak was gone. He told himself he could restart on Monday, then didn't.

3 February. The schedule was still on the fridge, but Tanvir had stopped looking at it. He told Aparna he'd "never been a gym person anyway," and pulled the membership card out of sight, feeling like he'd failed.

qa.q: What did Tanvir buy on 1 January?
qa.a: A year's gym membership.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel on 3 February when he put the membership card out of sight?
qa.a: Tanvir felt like a failure and avoided the reminder, hiding his disappointment behind a shrug.

qa.q: What could Tanvir do differently if he wants to restart, and why?
qa.a: Tanvir could plan two or three shorter sessions and allow for sick or busy weeks, because a plan that bends is likelier to survive than one that breaks.

qa.q: How might Aparna see Tanvir's plan from the beginning?
qa.a: Aparna raised an eyebrow on 1 January, so Aparna probably saw the plan as too big and now may see the disappointment as avoidable.

grounding: Motivated on 1 January, the person signs up for a year with hard daily workouts, then drops the whole plan after a cold and a busy week.

subtype: Approach: accountability with a friend and a shared log [Action]
passage:
In the office pantry, Kunal was refilling his bottle when Madhuri said, "I keep skipping my evening runs. Do you want to do this together?"

"I have the same problem," Kunal said. "Fine. Deal. Text me a photo the moment you finish, and I'll do the same."

They agreed on two fixed meetings at the park by the canteen, Tuesday and Saturday, and a shared note on their phones where each session got a tick. The next Tuesday it rained lightly and Kunal almost stayed in. Then his phone buzzed: Madhuri, already at the gate, holding two umbrellas.

He went. They walked, laughed at their own slowness, and both ticked the box.

qa.q: Which two days did Kunal and Madhuri agree to meet at the park?
qa.a: Tuesday and Saturday.

qa.q: What made Kunal go to the park despite the light rain?
qa.a: Kunal was tempted to stay in, but seeing Madhuri already at the gate made skipping feel like letting a friend down.

qa.q: What could Kunal and Madhuri do if one of them travels for work, and why?
qa.a: They could keep the messages going with a shorter session wherever they are, because the shared note keeps them accountable even apart.

qa.q: How might Madhuri see Kunal's agreement to the deal?
qa.a: Madhuri probably feels relieved that Kunal shares the same problem, as it turns a private struggle into something they can solve together.

grounding: Two colleagues agree to message after each session and meet at the park twice a week, with a shared record making skipping harder.

subtype: Approach: copy an influencer's routine and diet [Pitfall]
passage:
Kamal watched a video reel of a man who ate almost nothing and lifted enormous weights, and decided to copy him from Monday. It was exam season, his college was an hour away by bus, and he had never lifted anything heavier than a bag. He didn't care.

The first week, he skipped two meals and made himself lift until his arms shook. By Thursday every step felt like torture, and hunger made him snap at his cousin Pranav over nothing.

"That man has a different body, a different day and probably a coach," Pranav said. "You have a viva on Friday." Kamal ignored him. Ten days later, sore and starving, he quit everything and told nobody why.

qa.q: How far was Kamal's college by bus?
qa.a: An hour away.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling when he snapped at Pranav?
qa.a: Kamal was hungry, sore and irritable, and pushing hard to prove he could follow the plan.

qa.q: What could Kamal do instead of copying the reel, and why?
qa.a: Kamal could build a plan around his own timetable and start light, because a routine that fits his body and schedule is more likely to last.

qa.q: How does Pranav see Kamal's plan?
qa.a: Pranav sees a plan borrowed from someone with a different body and different demands, and is worried about Kamal during exams.

grounding: The person follows a reel plan of extreme cuts and heavy lifts without regard to body or schedule, and quits within two weeks.

subtype: Approach: pre-mortem on why the habit may fail [Thinking]
passage:
Bidisha, you asked how I kept going this time. The trick was thinking about quitting before I started. I sat down and pictured myself in a month, having stopped. Why? I wrote the reasons: late meetings that ate my evenings, the monsoon, and being too tired to move.

Then I gave each one a plan. Late meetings: a twenty-minute home routine that needs no shoes. Monsoon: the same routine indoors, and a walk when it clears. Tiredness: shift the session to early morning, and go to bed earlier on the days I have meetings. I'm Madhuri, and I honestly thought it was silly. But when the rain came in July, I was ready, and I didn't quit.

qa.q: What three reasons did Madhuri list for stopping?
qa.a: Late meetings, the monsoon and being too tired to move.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel about the exercise of imagining quitting?
qa.a: Madhuri thought it was silly at first, showing some doubt, before it proved useful when the rain came.

qa.q: What could Madhuri do if a new obstacle appears that the list did not cover, and why?
qa.a: Madhuri could add it to the list with a plan of its own, because the list is a living tool that improves as real problems appear.

qa.q: How might Bidisha see Madhuri's method?
qa.a: Bidisha may find it practical and surprising, since planning for failure at the start is not the usual way people think about staying motivated.

grounding: The person imagines quitting in a month and lists causes such as late meetings, the monsoon and tiredness, giving each a plan.

subtype: Approach: track and adjust after a missed week [Revision]
passage:
"Bhaiya, you missed the whole week," Sunaina said, leaning on the kitchen door. "So that's it? You're quitting?"

"No." Lokesh pulled out his notebook. "I looked at the ticks. Every session I skipped was in the evening. Late meetings, tired, hungry. The mornings, I never missed."

"So?"

"So it's not me, it's the timing. I'm moving everything to six-thirty in the morning."

"And if you miss again?"

"New rule. I can miss once, but never twice in a row."

Sunaina grinned. "You've turned a failure into a spreadsheet."

"It's data," he said. "Tomorrow, six-thirty. Bang on my door if I'm not up."

qa.q: What time will Lokesh move his sessions to?
qa.a: Six-thirty in the morning.

qa.q: What is Lokesh feeling after looking at his ticks?
qa.a: Lokesh feels determined and a bit relieved, since seeing the pattern shows the problem was timing and not a lack of effort.

qa.q: What could Lokesh do if the morning slot also fails, and why?
qa.a: Lokesh could note the reason again and test another time or a shorter session, because each missed session gives new information to adjust the plan.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see Lokesh's response to the missed week?
qa.a: Sunaina may be relieved and amused that Lokesh did not quit, and the joke about the spreadsheet shows a wish to help.

grounding: After missing a week, the person notes that late evenings fail, moves sessions to mornings and sets a never-miss-twice rule, treating the lapse as data.
